projects.title: ARTICULATE — AI-Powered Speech Accessibility Platform
projects.summary: Browser-based communication tool that transcribes atypical speech, repairs grammar while preserving meaning, and supports text-to-speech playback.
projects.opening: ARTICULATE helps people with atypical or unclear speech express themselves more confidently in real time. The platform records speech, transcribes it with a fine-tuned Whisper-based model, applies a Flan-T5 language model to repair grammar while preserving intended meaning, and provides clear text plus optional text-to-speech playback.
projects.problem: How can speech technology support clearer communication for people with dysarthria, Down syndrome, and other speech-related disabilities—without changing what they mean to say?
projects.role: Developed the accessible browser application, integrated speech recognition and language-repair pipelines, and designed human-centered UX for users, caregivers, teachers, and speech-language pathologists.
methods: Fine-tuned Whisper-based speech recognition
Flan-T5 grammar repair with meaning preservation
Text-to-speech playback pipeline
High-contrast mode, live waveform feedback, and simplified controls
Lazy model loading and fallback API handling
projects.results: Delivered an end-to-end accessible communication workflow in the browser, designed for real-time use by people with speech disabilities and the professionals who support them.
projects.learned: Accessibility is not a feature layer—it shapes model choice, latency, feedback design, and failure handling from the start.

projects.title: STATERA: Preventing Falls with Galvanic Vestibular Stimulation
projects.subtitle: A STEM II project focused on detecting and correcting balance issues before a fall happens.
projects.summary: For STEM II, my group built a glasses-mounted device that detects balance issues and uses galvanic vestibular stimulation to try to correct them before a fall happens.
projects.opening: For my STEM II class, each group was tasked with finding an issue in the community and coming up with a way to solve it. My group found that most devices meant to prevent falls only respond once the fall is already happening, there was not really anything that tried to correct someone's balance before they fell. We looked through a lot of possible technologies and I found galvanic vestibular stimulation, or GVS, which uses electrodes to apply a small current through the vestibular system and shift someone's perceived balance. From there we worked on combining GVS with a set of IMUs that could detect position and orientation, with everything connected through an ESP32.
projects.problem: Most fall prevention devices react when someone is already falling, so we wanted to see if a device could recognize the signs earlier and help correct the person's balance before the fall happened.
projects.role: I found GVS as the technology we ended up using, and a lot of my work was on the electronics behind the prototype. This included placing and connecting the IMUs, working with the ESP32, designing a PCB in EasyEDA, and helping with the testing and later iterations. The PCB especially took a lot of trial and error to get right.
methods: Three strategically placed MPU-6050 IMUs to track position and orientation
An ESP32 that collected the sensor data and controlled the system
A custom PCB designed in EasyEDA after a lot of testing and revision
Electrodes placed near the vestibular system to deliver GVS
A 3D-printed glasses frame and rechargeable battery so everything could be worn
50 controlled trials to test the balance detection and stimulation
projects.results: By the end, the system classified balance events with 88% accuracy across 50 trials, and the stimulation was detected in every active trial. We were also able to keep the prototype within the cost goal we set at the beginning.
projects.learned: This project taught me a lot about how different the first version of an idea can be from the thing that eventually works. PCB design was probably the clearest example of that, because it took multiple attempts and problems that I did not expect, and the testing process ended up being just as important as actually building the device.

projects.title: Finite Element Methods for the One-Dimensional Quantum Harmonic Oscillator
projects.subtitle: Turning a quantum equation into a computable model.
projects.summary: Numerical physics research comparing linear and Hermite finite elements for the quantum harmonic oscillator—part of the WPI Quantum research group internship.
projects.organization: Worcester Polytechnic Institute · Quantum Research Group
projects.opening: As part of the research group internship at WPI for Quantum, I used the finite element method to approximate the energy eigenvalues and wavefunctions of the one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator. The work compared lower-order linear elements with higher-order Hermite elements—including quintic Hermite bases—and evaluated how numerical choices affect accuracy.
projects.problem: How accurately can finite element methods reproduce a quantum system with known analytical energy levels?
projects.role: Research intern in the WPI Quantum group—developed and compared FEM implementations, validated results against analytical solutions, and documented numerical tradeoffs in a research paper.
methods: Spatial discretization of the quantum harmonic oscillator domain
Generalized eigenvalue formulation
Linear finite elements (N = 300, L = 8)
Cubic Hermite finite elements (N = 60, L = 8)
Comparison with known energy eigenvalues and wavefunction behavior
projects.results: Both approaches reproduced the expected energy spectrum; cubic Hermite elements achieved extremely high accuracy with far fewer degrees of freedom. Linear FEM first six energies: 0.500089, 1.500444, 2.501155, 3.502221, 4.503642, 5.505417. Cubic Hermite: 0.500000, 1.500000, 2.500001, 3.500004, 4.500010, 5.500021.
projects.learned: A physical equation becomes a numerical model through domain choice, basis construction, matrix assembly, eigenvalue solution, and rigorous validation against theory.

projects.title: HiMCM 2025: Firefighter Building Sweep Model
projects.subtitle: A hazard-aware model for deciding where firefighters should search, and when those decisions need to change.
projects.summary: For HiMCM 2025, my group and I modeled how firefighters could sweep a building quickly while fire, smoke, blocked paths, and incomplete information were all changing around them.
projects.opening: For HiMCM 2025, my group and I worked on the firefighter problem, where we had to figure out the most efficient way to sweep a building while still making sure every room was actually checked. The layout we were given was a one-floor office with six rooms, two exits, and two firefighters, which sounds fairly simple until fire, smoke, blocked paths, and incomplete information all start changing while the sweep is happening. We started with that smaller case and then kept making the model more realistic, eventually testing it on a two-floor building and a much more complicated 24-room, three-floor building.
projects.problem: What order should firefighters search the rooms in, where should they enter, and how many firefighters are actually useful once the conditions inside the building can change?
projects.role: My group and I built the model in three stages. We started with a static weighted graph, then made the travel costs change as hazards got worse, and finally added uncertain information, communication delays, congestion, and the ability to reassign firefighters while the sweep was still happening. We also had to make sure every room was verified by two different firefighters, since being fast does not really matter if a room can get missed.
methods: Represented rooms, hallways, exits, and stairs as a weighted graph
Used shortest-path calculations for the baseline model and changed edge costs as fire, smoke, debris, and visibility got worse
Assigned and reassigned firefighters based on the rooms that still needed to be checked
Estimated the likely fire origin from smoke and visibility reports when the starting location was unknown
Tested different crew sizes and entrance placements instead of assuming that adding more firefighters would always help
Required every room to be checked by two different firefighters
projects.results: The model produced room orders, routes, entrance assignments, and a minimum useful crew size for each layout. On the largest layout the biggest improvements happened when going from one to around five firefighters, after that the benefit kept getting smaller and eventually mostly flattened out. We also found that a hazard weight of 0.7 gave the best balance in our tests between taking a short route and avoiding dangerous parts of the building. Our paper received a Meritorious award in HiMCM, which put it in the top 13% internationally, and we advanced to IM²C.
projects.learned: A lot of the work was figuring out what “optimal” was even supposed to mean here, because the shortest route is not necessarily the route you would want a firefighter to take, and adding more people can create congestion instead of fixing the problem. We also had to be honest about where the model stops being realistic, especially because the hazard curves and layouts were simulated and not data from a real fire.

projects.title: Density-Dependent Model for the Phase-Out of Penny Acceptance
projects.summary: Diffusion model forecasting how businesses may stop accepting pennies after U.S. production ends, with cash-rounding economic analysis.
projects.opening: Developed a mathematical model forecasting how businesses may stop accepting pennies after U.S. penny production ends. Penny acceptance was modeled as a density-dependent diffusion process, capturing how urban, suburban, and rural businesses transition at different rates.
projects.problem: How will penny acceptance diffuse across regions with different population densities—and what are the economic tradeoffs of cash-rounding strategies?
projects.role: Formulated nonlinear differential equations, integrated population-density distributions, and extended the model to evaluate rounding strategies.
methods: Density-dependent diffusion process
Urban, suburban, and rural adoption rate modeling
Nonlinear differential equations with regional distributions
Cash-rounding profitability threshold analysis
projects.results: Projected substantially faster penny phase-out in dense areas than rural communities. Cash-rounding analysis identified a price threshold where rounding up becomes more profitable than rounding down.
projects.learned: Seemingly simple policy transitions hide spatial heterogeneity that only diffusion-style models make visible.

projects.title: Coverage-Oriented Patrol Routing for Rhino Anti-Poaching in Etosha
projects.subtitle: Team-orienteering routes on Etosha’s real road network
projects.summary: Research paper on routing limited ranger patrols to cover rhino poaching risk in Etosha National Park—multi-depot team orienteering on OpenStreetMap roads.
projects.opening: Rhino poaching in Namibia intensified through the mid-2020s, and Etosha National Park absorbed a large share of the losses. Once deterrents such as dehorning and arrests are in place, the remaining operational lever is patrol efficiency: given limited vehicles, fuel, and ranger-hours, where should patrols drive? This paper builds a coverage-oriented routing model on Etosha’s real road network, using poaching-risk and habitat fields from an antecedent spatial model (Model-1).
projects.problem: How can a fixed set of time-budgeted ranger patrols be routed on Etosha’s actual roads to maximize coverage of cells where poaching risk and rhino habitat coincide?
projects.role: Corresponding author. Led formulation of the multi-depot team-orienteering model, integration with the Model-1 risk/habitat surfaces, OR-Tools routing experiments, baseline comparisons, and sensitivity analysis.
methods: 805-cell, 5 km grid with modelled poaching risk × habitat-integrity rewards from Model-1
Multi-depot team orienteering on 419 real OpenStreetMap road segments
Time-budgeted loops from five ranger camps (Okaukuejo, Halali, Namutoni, Dolomite, Onkoshi)
Google OR-Tools guided local search with greedy, risk-only, habitat-only, and random baselines
Sensitivity tests on candidate set, budget, and up to 15% risk-map noise
projects.results: Five eight-hour patrols traversed cells covering about 26% of mapped risk-reward and 70–80% of the highest-priority cells, beating all four baselines and remaining essentially unchanged under 15% risk-map noise. A marginal-value test found a second patrol adds most at the western Okaukuejo and Dolomite stations. Framed as a modelling prototype that still needs validation against observed ranger movement before deployment.
projects.learned: Anti-poaching routing works best when the objective is inverted from ordinary navigation—maximize hazard covered, not minimize travel—and when risk surfaces are stress-tested for modest input error.

methods: Authored a comprehensive 20-page operational proposal and secured official administrative and principal approval

projects.results: Delivered a fully sponsored competitive math tournament with school approval, structured teams, and a seamless participant experience from check-in through awards.
projects.learned: Large student events succeed when fundraising, written proposals, and day-of logistics are treated as one project—not separate afterthoughts.
